definition: Dearth means a scarcity or lack of something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dearth. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dearth should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: City council members admitted that the dearth of affordable apartments was quietly pushing young families out of the neighborhoods where they grew up.
A shortage means there is not quite enough to go around, while a dearth is a serious, noticeable scarcity of something needed.
A dearth means very little of something exists, but an absence means there is none of it at all.

Scarcity is the general condition in which something is hard to obtain at all: water is scarce in a desert, for everyone, all the time. A dearth is a serious, noticeable lack of something needed, felt in one particular place or situation rather than everywhere.

Paucity means a smallness of amount or number, and it usually measures abstract things like evidence, ideas, or data. A dearth is the more urgent word: a serious lack of something needed. A study can show a paucity of data, while a region suffers a dearth of doctors.

A lack is the plain, neutral state of being without something, whether or not that absence matters much. A dearth is never neutral: it names a serious scarcity of something genuinely needed, one that people feel and complain about. Any missing thing is a lack; a dearth hurts.

an amount beyond what is needed
The shelter puppy's endearing habit of tilting its head won over the entire staff, and endearing grows from the same root, dear, that centuries ago gave English the word dearth.
Dearth means a scarcity or lack of something.
When the youth orchestra held spring auditions, forty violinists showed up but not a single oboist.
Facing such a dearth of oboe players, the conductor joked that he might have to rewrite the entire symphony around the instruments he actually had.
The orchestra has plenty of some musicians but a serious scarcity of oboists, and that shortage of something needed is exactly what a dearth is.

Dearth almost always appears in the pattern 'a dearth of' followed by a noun, as in 'a dearth of evidence' or 'a dearth of options.' Despite growing out of the word dear, it has nothing to do with affection today; its natural opposite is a glut or surplus.

Every autumn, the Harlow County youth soccer league prints its schedule in September and spends October apologizing for it.
The problem is not fields, and it is not players — registration climbs every year.
The problem is a dearth of referees.
Two seasons ago the county certified forty officials; this fall, eleven remain.
Games are postponed weekly, and coaches have begun refereeing one another's matches, badly.
League director Amara Osei is blunt about why it stings: the shortage is local.
Three neighboring counties, which pay travel stipends, have waiting lists of certified referees.
Parents feel the gap every Saturday, and the league's board now calls it the single threat that could end the season.
